print-comments-and-errors.label: Print, Comments, and First Errors
print-comments-and-errors.summary: Display text with print(), add comments for readers, and repair simple syntax mistakes.

sc-print-purpose.title: What print() does
sc-print-purpose.hint: `print()` is used when a program needs to show a value.

help.concept: `print()` displays the value passed inside its parentheses. The quote marks make `Hello` a string value.
help.hint_1: The line runs normally; it is neither a comment nor an input request.
help.hint_2: Choose the result that would appear in the output panel.

options.b: Hello is stored for later without being shown.
options.d: Python waits for the user to type Hello.

sc-comment-line.title: Recognize a Python comment
sc-comment-line.prompt: Which line is a Python comment?
sc-comment-line.hint: Python uses `#` to begin a comment.

help.concept: A comment begins with `#`. Python ignores the comment text when it runs the program.
help.hint_1: A quoted string is still a value, not a comment.
help.hint_2: Look for the line whose first meaningful character is `#`.

mc-valid-print-lines.title: Find valid print calls
mc-valid-print-lines.prompt: Which lines are valid Python `print()` calls? Choose all correct answers.
mc-valid-print-lines.hint: Check the parentheses and quote marks in every line.

help.concept: A basic `print()` call needs the function name, an opening `(`, a valid value such as a quoted string, and a matching closing `)`.
help.hint_1: Python accepts both single and double quotes for strings.
help.hint_2: Reject lines with an unclosed string or an unclosed function call.

mc-comments-behavior.title: Understand comment behavior
mc-comments-behavior.prompt: Which statements about Python comments are true? Choose all correct answers.
mc-comments-behavior.hint: Think about both Python's behavior and why programmers write comments.

help.concept: Comments begin with `#`, are ignored during execution, and can document code for people reading it.
help.hint_1: Comments do not appear as normal program output.
help.hint_2: Select the syntax fact, the execution fact, and the reader-facing purpose.

options.b: A comment is automatically printed as program output.
options.c: Python ignores comment text when executing the program.
options.d: A comment can explain code to someone reading it.

dr-build-valid-print.title: Build a print call
dr-build-valid-print.prompt: Arrange the tokens to create valid Python code that prints `Hi`.
dr-build-valid-print.hint: Start with the function name, then open the call.

help.concept: A function call follows the pattern `name(value)`.
help.hint_1: The string value belongs between the opening and closing parentheses.

ci-print-one-line.title: Print one exact line
ci-print-one-line.prompt:
Write one line of Python that prints exactly:

`Welcome to Python`

help.concept: `print()` displays the string value passed to it.
help.hint_1: Capitalization and spaces must match the required output.
help.hint_2: Use one `print(...)` call containing the complete message in quotes.

0.message: Use one print call containing the exact string Welcome to Python.

ci-comment-and-output.title: Add a useful comment without changing output
ci-comment-and-output.prompt:
The starter program already prints `Ready`. Add one useful Python comment on the line above the existing `print()` statement describing what the program is showing.

Do not change the program output. Only `Ready` should appear.
ci-comment-and-output.hint: Add a line beginning with `#` above the existing print statement.

help.concept: A comment documents the source code for a reader without becoming normal program output.
help.hint_2: Your new first line should start with `#` and explain the purpose.

ci-comment-and-output.solutionCode:
# Show that the program is ready
print("Ready")

ci-fix-missing-paren.title: Repair a missing parenthesis
ci-fix-missing-paren.prompt:
The starter code has a syntax error because the `print()` call is not closed. Fix the code so it prints exactly:

`Hello`
ci-fix-missing-paren.hint: Match the opening `(` with its closing symbol.

help.concept: Python must be able to match the opening and closing parentheses of a function call before it can run the program.
help.hint_2: Add the missing closing parenthesis at the end of the line.

0.message: Close the existing print call so it displays Hello.

fb-close-print-call.title: Close the print call
fb-close-print-call.prompt: Choose the missing symbol that makes this line valid Python.
fb-close-print-call.hint: The opening parenthesis after `print` needs a matching partner.

help.concept: Parentheses in a function call must be balanced. A missing closing parenthesis prevents Python from reading the statement correctly.
help.hint_1: The string itself is already complete.
help.hint_2: Choose the symbol that closes the `(` after `print`.

sketch-print-basics.title: Use print() to display output
sketch-print-basics.bodyMarkdown:
`print()` lets a Python program show a value in the output.

```python
print("Hello")
print("Welcome to Python")
```

Output:

```text
Hello
Welcome to Python
```

Each call to `print()` above displays one string and then moves to a new output line.

The text inside the parentheses is a **string literal**, so it needs quotes:

```python
print("Ready")
```

Think of the line in two parts:

- `print(...)` means **display this value**
- `"Ready"` is the value to display

**Predict before running:** What two lines appear if the program contains `print("A")` followed by `print("B")`?

sketch-comments.title: Comments explain code without producing output
sketch-comments.bodyMarkdown:
A **comment** is a note for people reading the code.

In Python, a comment begins with `#`:

```python
# Show the program status
print("Ready")
```

Output:

```text
Ready
```

Python ignores the comment when it executes the program. The comment helps a reader understand why the next line exists, but it does not become output.

Comments are useful when they explain purpose:

```python
# Show the title before the lesson begins
print("Python Basics")
```

A comment should add useful context rather than repeat the code word for word.

**Check yourself:** In the example above, which line is for the reader and which line produces output?

sketch-first-errors.title: Repair a simple syntax error
sketch-first-errors.bodyMarkdown:
Python code has to follow a valid structure before it can run.

This line is incomplete:

```python
print("Hello"
```

The `print(` call opens a parenthesis but never closes it. Python cannot finish reading the statement, so the program stops with a **syntax error**.

The corrected line is:

```python
print("Hello")
```

Strings also need matching quote marks. This is broken:

```python
print("Hello)
```

and this is complete:

```python
print("Hello")
```

When a short line has a syntax error, check its pairs:

- opening and closing parentheses: `(` and `)`
- opening and closing quotes: `"..."`

The next error-focused lesson will go deeper into reading error messages. Here, the goal is simply to recognize and repair an incomplete statement.
